gaps.text: In-line measurement of Temperature at the measurement point with temperature sensor

Combining several spectroscopy methods (data fusion) (Start from one model per method and fuse the joined spectra with block scaling, because variables from different methods are not equivalent and a method with more variables would otherwise dominate. The MIR ATR and Raman measurements must come from the same small spot and be normalised to a common time step, and each instrument keeps its own calibration and maintenance. The fused model must beat the best single method on independent runs, otherwise the second instrument is dropped.)
No supplied source gives a detection limit, accuracy or response time for residual butyl acrylate, in an emulsion polymerisation or in any similar matrix.
No supplied source addresses the fluorescence behaviour of anionic surfactants or persulfate initiators.

items.finding: The source states that temperature sensitivity of OH bands is a severe drawback for measuring aqueous solutions in NIR and MIR, making tempered sample holders necessary.
items.how_it_applies: For a water-based emulsion, temperature at the measurement point may affect MIR spectra, so test whether temperature control or logging is needed at the probe.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The source is a review in biopharmaceutical downstream processing, not emulsion polymerisation; tempered sample holders are laboratory/off-line and may not transfer directly to an in-line probe.

citation.quote: Additionally, the temperature sensitivity of the OH bands is a severe drawback for measuring aqueous solution in NIR and MIR, which makes tempered sample holders necessary [29].
citation.label: E02 ¶12

items.finding: The source varied concentrations, ionic strength and temperature to obtain a robust model.
items.how_it_applies: This suggests temperature should be varied or recorded during calibration so the model can be robust to process temperature changes.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The study is on reactive liquid-liquid extraction in lithium recycling, not emulsion polymerisation, and it does not describe an in-line temperature sensor.

citation.quote: The concentrations of nitric acid and hydrochloric acid as well as the ionic strength and temperature were varied to obtain a robust model.
citation.label: E01 ¶19

items.finding: Low-level data fusion is described as the simplest way to combine inputs by placing variables from different sources one after the other in a new data matrix.
items.how_it_applies: This could inform a first fusion test by concatenating MIR and Raman variables, but the need for block scaling must be checked separately.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The source is a general PAT data-fusion review, not MIR/Raman on emulsion polymerisation; concatenation alone does not guarantee improved prediction.

citation.quote: Low-level data fusion (LLDF) is considered the simplest method to achieve a combination of inputs. In this case, the data is rearranged into a new data matrix, where the variables coming from different sources are placed one after the other.
citation.label: E03 ¶31

items.finding: A Raman and FT-IR food analytical study found that instrument complementarity was not always sufficient to improve predictive performance for several CQAs.
items.how_it_applies: This supports requiring the fused MIR/Raman model to beat the best single method on independent runs before keeping the second instrument.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The cited study is in food analysis, not emulsion polymerisation; the result may not transfer to butyl acrylate in a milky white matrix.

citation.quote: In some situations, instrument complementarity (not data complementarity) was not sufficient to improve the performance of predictive several CQAs, as shown by a Raman and FT-IR data based food analytical study [73].
citation.label: E03 ¶36
